newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Zinc bubble bursts on London Metal Exchange.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Zinc bubble bursts on London Metal Exchange.

text.p: A speculative bubble in the price of zinc burst spectacularly on the London Metal Exchange (LME) on Tuesday, dropping almost 20 percent in one hour.
This overshadowed all other events in commodity markets although other base metals were also busy while coffee and some grain markets were firmer.

Talk among metal traders that Chinese smelters had managed to cover their commitments to the London Metal Exchange zinc market was sufficient to cast doubt on the validity of recent very high prices which saw a seven-year high of $1,674 a tonne set Monday.
"All that was holding the market up here was expectations of huge Chinese buying orders having to come into the market before September," a trade source said.
Conflicting reports from China as to whether the positions had been covered or not increased market turmoil and sent investment funds into a headlong flight to lock-in some of their profits.
But once buyers smelt potential panic in the air they backed-off very sharply in anticipation of being able to fulfill their own orders at much cheaper levels.
This resulted in a near $300 drop in one hour of morning business before the fall halted and prices gyrated for the rest of the day.
"We're now in a limbo period....uncertainty prevails until the air clears," analyst Angus MacMillan of metal brokers Billiton Metals said.

One pointer that convinced some traders that the Chinese still had positions to cover was that the premiums for nearby delivery zinc continued to hold firm, indicating that periods of potential supply tightness still existed.

Elswhere on the LME nickel prices surged by $100 as the market entered a nervous period in the build-up to a labour contract expiry at Canadian number two nickel producer Falconbridge's, Sudbury, Ontario, facilities on Friday.
Union spokesman Rolly Gaulthier said wokers would strike if there was no deal by then, "There is either a deal or we're out," he said.
Coffee prices continued their recent rally with fund buying and shortcovering taking prices back up to levels ruling two-weeks ago before the latest sell-off.

The main factor appears to be a near term fear over the lack oa supplies available to the New York market but, in general, the overall supply situation appears to have eased given ample roaster stocks and slowing summer consumption.

In Chicago forecasts of a week of only minimal moisture in U.S.Midwest growing areas sent corn up by around eight cents a bushel to $2.60 on the Board of Trade and soyabeans by around 13 cents to $6.78 a bushel.
